meta.title: Who really said “The Difference Between Stupidity and Genius Is That Genius Has Its Limits”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein. The joke is Alexandre Dumas fils’, printed in French around 1865; Princeton’s Einstein reference files it under ‘Probably Not By Einstein’.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘The Difference Between Stupidity and Genius Is That Genius Has Its Limits’?
meta.ogDescription: Not Einstein — Alexandre Dumas fils, in print by about 1865. Elbert Hubbard sharpened it in 1906.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually Alexandre Dumas, fils
answer.sourceLine: The thought appears in French around 1865, in the entry for Bêtise (stupidity) in Pierre Larousse’s Grand Dictionnaire Universel du XIXe Siècle, credited there to ‘Alex. Dum.’ — Alexandre Dumas, fils. It reached English by 1890 in a list headed ‘Some of Dumas’s Maxims’, and the crisp modern phrasing is a later reshaping.

source.excerpt: Une chose qui m’humilie profondément est de voir que le génie humain a des limites, quand la bêtise humaine n’en a pas.
trail: Quote Investigator locates the French wording in volume 2 of Larousse’s Grand Dictionnaire Universel du XIXe Siècle, published circa 1865, under the entry Bêtise, attributed to ‘Alex. Dum.’ Read the investigation ↗

The earliest English instance Quote Investigator found appeared in 1890 in The Travelers’ Record, in a list titled ‘Some of Dumas’s Maxims’ credited to L’Echo de Paris; a version in The Phrenological Journal the following year names ‘A. Dumas, fils’ specifically. The 1890 and 1891 citations ↗
Princeton University Press’s reference The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, edited by Alice Calaprice, lists the saying in its section ‘Probably Not By Einstein’. QI cites the Calaprice entry ↗

Quote Investigator’s conclusion credits Dumas fils with the 1865 expression and Elbert Hubbard with popularising the sharpened 1906 version, and states there is no substantive evidence Einstein said any of them. QI’s conclusion ↗
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator gives this English rendering: ‘One thing that humbles me deeply is to see that human genius has its limits while human stupidity does not.’ The earliest English printing it found, in 1890, reads: ‘What distresses me is to see that human genius has limits and human stupidity none.’

author.name: Alexandre Dumas, fils
author.heading: About Alexandre Dumas, fils
author.bio: Alexandre Dumas, fils was the son of the novelist who wrote The Three Musketeers, and a major writer in his own right: his novel and play La Dame aux Camélias became the basis for Verdi’s La Traviata. In later life he was known as much for his moralising essays and epigrams as for his drama, and it is from that vein of aphorism that this line comes — collected into a French dictionary entry on stupidity while he was still alive.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A nineteenth-century French epigram that drifted onto the twentieth century’s most quotable scientist.

items.why: Quote Investigator finds the Einstein ascription no earlier than 1994 — thirty-nine years after his death in 1955 — and Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein places it under ‘Probably Not By Einstein’. Quote Investigator ↗

The American writer and publisher printed ‘Genius may have its limitations, but stupidity is not thus handicapped’ in The Philistine in 1906; it was reprinted the next year as a Hubbard epigram. Quote Investigator credits him with popularising, not originating. The 1906 citation ↗
Credited as ‘Alex. Dum.’ in the circa-1865 Larousse dictionary entry, and by name in an 1891 journal printing. The 1865 citation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Dumas fils’, from around 1865 — fourteen years before Einstein was born. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Dumas fils was the author of La Dame aux Camélias and, in his later years, a moralist much given to epigrams. The line reads as a Parisian salon joke, and that is roughly what it was: a maxim collected into a dictionary entry on stupidity.

Its journey to Einstein is the standard route. A funny observation about intelligence loses its author, drifts for a century, and finally lands on whichever name means ‘clever’ to the largest number of people. Einstein has absorbed more of these than anyone; Princeton’s scholarly edition of his quotations needs a whole section for them.
context.pull: A funny line about intelligence will eventually find its way to Einstein.

sourcesVerified.claim: The French wording appears circa 1865 in Larousse's Grand Dictionnaire Universel, vol. 2, entry 'Betise', p. 650, credited to 'Alex. Dum.'
QI concludes Alexandre Dumas fils can be credited with the expression and that there is no substantive evidence Einstein said it.
'The Ultimate Quotable Einstein' (Princeton UP) lists the saying under 'Probably Not By Einstein'.
Elbert Hubbard printed a 'not thus handicapped' version in The Philistine in 1906.
Alexandre Dumas fils lived 1824-1895 and was a French dramatist and novelist.
